endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Ensure that users understand that no bug fixes, updates, patches, or technical support will be available once end-of-life (EOL) is signed off [39].

endorsements.title: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance)
endorsements.quote: A description of how the modifications were implemented and a description of how users will be informed of implemented modifications such as updated instructions for use or a version history.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: A description of the procedures for communicating the results of performance monitoring

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: This decision point features guides for disseminating information about AI products to affected clinicians and managing changes in the work environment caused by AI products put into clinical use.

endorsements.title: The 'Hippocratic Oath' for AI-based clinical decision support systems
endorsements.issuer: BMC medical informatics and decision making
endorsements.quote: Users must be notified of these changes and significant alterations to functionality will require new evaluation studies to be carried out.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether notifying clinicians of AI model changes, monitoring findings, mitigations, or end-of-life status changes clinician behavior or patient outcomes, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support for R217 rests on five endorsements, two of them FDA guidance documents, which describe the practice as expected conduct.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The five endorsements are a framework, two guidance documents, a decision-point guide, and a commentary. Under GRADE conventions, expert and regulatory statements do not supply outcome evidence, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

FDA's final guidance on predetermined change control plans asks manufacturers to describe how users will be informed of modifications, such as updated instructions for use or a version history. The draft lifecycle guidance asks for procedures to communicate monitoring results. These duties fall on manufacturers, so deployers may need their own process to relay that information to clinicians.

The hazard, clinicians applying outdated expectations after a tool changes, is plausible, but no supplied study measures how often it occurs or what harm follows. Without such data, a deployer cannot estimate how many errors a notification process would intercept or which change types most warrant alerts.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often clinicians are unaware of AI model updates, retraining, or retirement, and whether structured notification (version histories, alerts, or training refreshers) changes clinician reliance, override rates, or error rates compared with no notification. Studies should also compare notification channels and frequencies for their effect on alert fatigue.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether notification processes reach clinicians in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy care settings. Safety-net deployers with fewer informatics staff may find it harder to relay vendor change notices, and this possibility remains untested.
